parts.title: Part 1
parts.context: A man phones the organiser of a craft fair to book a stall.
script: Good morning, Harbour Lane Craft Fair office, Hana speaking. How can I help?
Oh, hello. I'm calling about taking a stall at the summer fair. I saw the poster in the library, but it didn't say much about how to book.
No, it's all done through the office. I can take your details now if you like. Have you traded with us before?
No, this would be my first time. I've only sold at school fairs up to now.
That's fine, we get a lot of new people. Can I start with your name?
And could you spell the surname for me?
Of course. It's P-R-E-W-I-T-T. Two Ts at the end, which people often forget.
Got it. And a contact number?
07811 640 293. Thank you. And what will you be selling?
Mostly handmade candles. I make a few soaps as well, but the candles are the main thing.

Lovely. Candles are always popular, though I should say we already have two other candle makers booked, so we'll put you at the opposite end of the field. Now, the fair runs over the whole weekend, but you can book either day or both. Which would you prefer?
Well, I was thinking Saturday, because I assumed that would be the busier day.
It is a bit busier in the morning, yes, but honestly the Sunday crowd spends more, because they tend to stay for the whole afternoon. Plenty of our regulars say Sunday is the better day.
Oh, right. In that case I'll go for Sunday, please. Just the one day to begin with.
Sunday it is. Now, stalls come in two sizes. The standard one is 3 metres wide and 2 metres deep. The larger one is 4 metres wide, but the depth is the same.
And what's the difference in price?
The standard stall is 35 pounds for the day, and the larger one is 45 pounds.
I think I'll start with the smaller one, then. Ten pounds extra is a lot when I don't know how sales will go.
That's sensible. So that's the standard stall, 3 metres by 2. The price includes a table and a gazebo to keep the rain off, but you'll need to bring your own chair and a cloth for the table.
That's no problem, I've got a cloth. Do I need a licence or anything like that?

No licence, but because you're selling candles we do need to see a certificate of public liability insurance. Lots of people think their home insurance covers it, but it usually doesn't, so do check with your provider. You can just email us a copy.
Right, I'll get that sorted this week. Thanks for warning me.
Now, I've put you on stall 18. That's right next to the bandstand, which is a good spot, because people stop to listen to the music and then have a wander round the stalls nearby.
That sounds great. Is there anything I should know about getting set up?

Yes. The gates open for stallholders at 7.30, and the fair opens to the public at 10.00. Some people turn up at 8, but by then the car park is nearly full and you end up carrying everything a long way.
OK, 7.30. I'll aim for that, then. Is there anything to pay now?
Not today. I'll email you the booking form and a map of the field this afternoon, and you can pay when you send the insurance certificate back. Could you give me your email address?
Yes, it's oliver at wickerandwax dot co dot uk.
Perfect. I'll get that off to you straight away. Thank you for calling, Oliver, and good luck with the candles.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.context: A mountain rescue volunteer gives a talk on staying safe when hill walking.
script: Good evening, everyone, and thanks for coming along. I'm Greg Moran, and I've been a volunteer with Brackendale Mountain Rescue for fifteen years. Tonight I'd like to talk about staying safe when you're walking in the hills, and I'll try to keep it practical.

Let me start with some numbers. Last year our team was called out 96 times. That's up from 69 the year before, although the year before that was our busiest ever, with 112 call-outs, when the weather was unusually good and the hills were crowded.

So what causes all these call-outs? People tend to assume that most of them involve a terrible storm or a serious fall, and of course we do deal with both. But the biggest single cause is much more ordinary. It's walkers who set off too late and are still on the hill when it gets dark. Injuries come second, and bad weather only comes third.

Now, planning. Everyone knows you should tell someone where you're going. What I'd add is that you should also tell them when you expect to be back, and when they should call us if you haven't returned. A route card left with a friend, or on the dashboard of your car, is ideal. Some people think they should register with the visitor centre as well, but there's no system for that, so please don't rely on it. And a text message from the summit is a nice extra, but it's no substitute, because up there you may well have no signal at all.

Next, the weather. A lot of walkers look at the forecast for the nearest town, and that tells you very little. On the tops it can be 10 degrees colder than in the valley, and the wind is far stronger. Always look at the mountain forecast, which gives you conditions at the summit, and pay particular attention to the wind speed. A forecast from the day before is fine for planning, but do check it again on the morning of your walk.

I'm often asked whether the smartphone has made the paper map obsolete. Well, it's a brilliant tool. You can download maps to use offline, and an app can give you your grid reference in seconds. But there's a catch. Phone batteries lose their charge much faster in the cold, so keep yours inside a warm pocket close to your body, not in the side of your rucksack, and don't use it for music or videos on the way up.
Now let me go through five items of equipment, because this is where I see the same mistakes again and again.

First, boots. Shiny new boots straight from the shop are a recipe for blisters. Whatever you buy, wear them around the house and on short walks for a few weeks beforehand, so they're properly worn in before the big day.

Second, your waterproof jacket. Most jackets lose their water resistance over time, as dirt clogs the fabric. Don't throw yours away. A wash with a special cleaning product, followed by a quick treatment, will restore the coating, and it costs far less than a new jacket.

Third, the map and compass. I meet so many people who carry a compass but have never actually used one. A hillside in thick cloud is the wrong place to learn. Spend an afternoon in a local park practising, so that the skills are second nature when you need them.
Fourth, a head torch. Even in summer, carry one. Check it before every trip, and replace the batteries each time, rather than waiting for them to fail halfway down a mountain.

And last, food. Some people say you should take twice as much as you think you need, but what matters more is that you can get at it. Keep your snacks in a pocket you can reach without taking your pack off. If it's a nuisance to stop, you simply won't eat, and tired walkers make poor decisions.

That's the main advice. If you remember only one thing from tonight, make it this: start early, and turn back in good time. The hill will still be there tomorrow. Now, I'd be happy to take questions, and we've got some route cards at the back for you to take away.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.context: Two students discuss a placement on an archaeological dig.
script: Josh, hi. Have you had a chance to read the placement pack for the Aldermoor dig?
I've skimmed it. I wanted to talk it through with you, to be honest, because we have to hand in our preferences by Friday.
Well, I've already made up my mind. I'm going for Aldermoor. I know a lot of people want the big coastal fort, the one with the famous director, but I couldn't care less who runs it.
So what's the attraction for you?

The geophysical survey. They run magnetometers over the whole field before anyone lifts a trowel, and they teach the students how to do it. Nobody on our course gets to try that until the third year, and I'd love to be able to say I've done it.
Right. I'll be honest, what drew me was the price. The camping fees are a fraction of what the other sites charge, so my loan will stretch a lot further.

What I'm nervous about is the recording side. I don't mind the digging at all. I spent two summers on a building site, so I can shift earth all day. But every layer has to be drawn to scale on a plan, and my drawing is hopeless. Last term my sketch of the pottery looked like a plate of spaghetti.
Dr Alvarez said they pair beginners with a supervisor for the first week, so you'll get plenty of help. And it's mostly about measuring carefully, not artistic talent.

Something else that's useful is that they record everything on tablets. The context sheets are filled in digitally and linked to the photographs. I looked at job adverts for archaeology technicians last week, and nearly every one asked for experience of digital recording. I think having that on my CV matters more than a letter from the director.
Maybe, though a good reference never hurts.
True. But it's the software that employers ask about.
OK. Shall we do some preparation before we go? We could go through last year's students' reports in the library.

I did look, but they're quite dry, and the placement has changed since then. What I'd suggest instead is the museum in town. They hold the finds from Aldermoor's first excavation in the 1960s, and the curator said we're welcome to look at them any Thursday.
Brilliant. We could go next week. Should we buy some kit as well?
I'd leave that for now. The pack says what to bring, and we don't want to spend money on things the site already supplies.
Good point. And how is it assessed? An essay again?

It was an essay up until last year, 3,000 words. Then they talked about a presentation to the department, but in the end they went for a daily field diary, handed in at the end, with a short reflection on top.
That's better. I'd rather write as I go than try to remember everything afterwards.
Same here. Right, the practical details. Let me find the page. Here we are. Boots first. It says everybody must wear steel-toed boots on site, and they won't let you work without them.
I'll need to buy a pair, then. Where do we sleep? In tents?
No, in shared caravans, four to a caravan, which I'm pleased about, as I hate camping in the rain.
Definitely. And what happens to the finds?
Each afternoon they're washed in the finds tent, then dried and sorted. You rotate between jobs, so everybody takes a turn.

Yes, on Friday afternoons there's a talk. This year it's on Roman pottery, given by a specialist from the university. It sounds quite good, actually, and it should help us to date the things we dig up.
The site supplies spades, wheelbarrows and buckets, but you have to bring your own trowel. They say a pointed one, and people get very attached to theirs.
Ha, I can imagine. I'll order one tonight.
Good. Then let's both email the placements office before Friday, and we'll put Aldermoor as our first choice.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.context: A lecturer talks about how languages die and how some have been revived.
script: Good afternoon, everyone. Today I want to talk about something most people never notice happening: the death of languages. And, more hopefully, about how some of them have been brought back.

Let's begin with the scale of the problem. There are about 7,000 languages in the world today, and experts estimate that one of them falls silent about every 2 weeks. Around 40 per cent are considered endangered, and many of those are spoken by only a few hundred people, most of whom are elderly.

You might assume that languages die because they are banned, and certainly there have been terrible cases of that, where children were punished at school for speaking their mother tongue. But the usual route is much quieter. A language begins to die when parents stop passing it on to their children. They may go on speaking it to each other, but they talk to the children in the dominant language, and within a generation or two there is nobody left to speak it.

Why would parents do that? People often blame migration to the cities, and that does play a part, but the main driver is economic. Think of a family in a remote village where the local language has no place in the school, the bank or the job market. Parents believe, quite reasonably, that their children will have better prospects if they speak the national language fluently. Sometimes there is also a feeling that the old language is old-fashioned, and that is a powerful force among teenagers.

Does it matter? Linguists say yes. When a language dies, a unique way of describing the world goes with it: knowledge of plants, of local weather, of histories that were only ever passed on by word of mouth.

Now for the hopeful part. Consider Manx, the Celtic language of the Isle of Man. Its last native speaker, Ned Maddrell, died in 1974, and many people declared the language extinct. But recordings of native speakers had been made before the last of them died, and those recordings, together with a small group of determined enthusiasts, allowed teaching to begin again. Today there is a Manx-language primary school, and children are growing up with the language.

A second example is New Zealand. By the early 1980s, Maori was in serious decline, and most children no longer spoke it. In 1982 the first Maori pre-schools opened, known as language nests. Elders, who still spoke the language fluently, looked after children under five and spoke only Maori to them. Within a few years, these children were entering primary school as confident speakers, and the movement spread to schools and later to broadcasting.

The most dramatic case of all is Hebrew. For nearly two thousand years it was used almost entirely for prayer. Nobody spoke it at home. Then, in the late nineteenth century, a scholar called Eliezer Ben-Yehuda decided it should become an everyday language again. People often imagine that a government or an institution made this happen, but it began with one man and his family. The language had no words for ordinary modern life, so he compiled a dictionary of new words, which gradually found their way into daily use. Today Hebrew has millions of native speakers.

Hawaiian offers a different lesson. After decades of decline, communities set up immersion schools, where everything is taught through Hawaiian. The programme grew year by year, until today a student can study every subject in the language, right up to university level.

Technology is now playing a part too. Many communities use mobile apps, social media and online dictionaries to reach young people who would never open a grammar book. A teenager who sees a funny video in her grandparents' language is far more likely to try speaking it.

So what do these successes have in common? The most important factor seems to be that the language is used at home, and not just in the classroom. Lessons alone are rarely enough. Where children hear the language from family members every day, it survives. Where it is something they only meet for an hour at school, it usually fades.

One last point. A revived language is never quite the same as the one that was lost. Because most new speakers grew up speaking something else, their pronunciation often shows the influence of that first language, and the grammar can change a little too. Some purists dislike this. But most linguists would say that a living, slightly changed language is far better than a perfectly preserved one that nobody speaks. Thank you.

passages.title: The history of the weather forecast
paras: A  For most of history, people predicted the weather from folklore: a red sky at night, the behaviour of animals, the ache in an old injury. Some of these sayings contain real observation, but none of them could say what would happen in three days' time, and few people imagined that it might be possible to do better. The idea that the weather could be forecast scientifically, and the word forecast itself, belong to the middle of the nineteenth century, and largely to one man, an English naval officer named Robert FitzRoy.

B  FitzRoy had captained HMS Beagle on the voyage that carried Charles Darwin around the world. In 1854 he was put in charge of a small government department whose task was to collect weather records from ships at sea. The work gained urgency in 1859, when a ferocious storm wrecked more than a hundred vessels around the British coast and cost hundreds of lives. FitzRoy was convinced that such disasters could be avoided if sailors were warned in time, and the means of doing so had only just arrived. The electric telegraph meant that observations of wind, pressure and cloud made in one place could reach another far faster than the weather itself could travel. By 1860 FitzRoy was receiving reports every morning from stations all round the coast, and he plotted them on maps to watch storms advance across the country. Before the telegraph, a ship's log might take months to reach an office; now a captain at a distant port could be told within hours that a gale was heading his way.

C  Gale warnings for ports were first sent out in February 1861, and in August of that year The Times printed the first daily weather forecast, a term FitzRoy himself invented because he disliked the word prophecy, which he thought unscientific. The response, however, was far from grateful. Most of his scientific colleagues considered forecasting little more than guesswork, and the newspapers took delight in printing his failures. Farmers and sailors complained when a predicted storm did not arrive, forgetting the lives that cautious warnings might have saved. FitzRoy died in 1865 and the public forecasts were suspended; they did not resume until 1879.

D  The next great advance was theoretical. In 1904 a Norwegian physicist, Vilhelm Bjerknes, argued that the atmosphere obeys the laws of physics and that, given its present state, its future state could in principle be calculated. The person who tried it was a British mathematician, Lewis Fry Richardson. Working entirely by hand, he spent about six weeks calculating the change in pressure at a single point in Europe over just six hours, using observations from one day in 1910. His answer was wildly wrong, predicting a rise in pressure that never happened. But the method was sound, and Richardson published it in 1922 with a striking suggestion: a forecast factory in which 64,000 human calculators, seated in a vast circular hall, would keep pace with the weather across the entire globe. Nobody took the proposal literally, but it described, with uncanny accuracy, how modern forecasting would work.

E  The factory became a reality of a kind in 1950, when a team of American meteorologists used one of the first electronic computers to produce a 24-hour forecast. The machine needed almost as long to complete the calculation as the weather did to happen, but the principle had been proved. A decade later another development transformed the supply of data. In April 1960 the United States launched the first weather satellite, whose television pictures showed cloud systems from above, including storms over remote oceans where no ship or station had ever made a report. For the first time, forecasters could see the whole pattern of the weather rather than a scatter of points on a map, and the tropical cyclones that had once appeared without warning could be tracked from the day they formed.

F  Better machines and better data did not, however, deliver the perfect forecast that some had expected. In the early 1960s the American meteorologist Edward Lorenz noticed that when he re-ran a computer simulation, entering a starting value rounded to three decimal places instead of six, the result was a completely different weather pattern after a few simulated weeks. Tiny errors in the starting conditions grow rapidly, a property that later became known as chaos. Because no measurement is ever perfect, there is a limit, of about two weeks, beyond which detailed forecasts cannot be made however powerful the computer. The same discovery explains why the weather in a particular place a month from now remains, in practice, unknowable.

G  Forecasters have learned to live with that limit. Today's models divide the atmosphere into millions of grid boxes and run on supercomputers that perform quadrillions of calculations a second. Rather than trust a single run, forecasters repeat the calculation dozens of times, each with slightly altered starting values, a method called ensemble forecasting. When most of the runs agree, confidence is high; when they scatter, the public is warned to expect uncertainty, which is why a forecast now speaks of a 70 per cent chance of rain rather than simply rain. The results are impressive. By one estimate, forecasts have gained roughly one day of useful accuracy every decade, so that the weather for next weekend is now predicted better than tomorrow's was in the days when FitzRoy's maps were pinned to the wall.

passages.title: How plants defend themselves
paras: A  A rabbit can run and a bird can fly, but a plant that is being eaten can do neither. Rooted to a single spot for its whole life, it must endure whatever comes along, from caterpillars and beetles to deer and elephants, and it must do so without a brain, without muscles and without an immune system of the kind that animals possess. Yet plants are far from defenceless. They have survived for hundreds of millions of years among hungry animals, and the reason is that they have evolved a remarkable range of defences, some of them astonishingly sophisticated. Biologists now regard the plant kingdom as an arena of constant chemical and mechanical warfare, almost all of it invisible to the casual observer.

B  The most obvious defences are physical. Thorns, spines and prickles discourage browsing mammals; thick bark protects tree trunks from gnawing; and hairs on the surface of leaves can trap or puncture small insects. Less visible is the strategy used by grasses, which draw silica, the mineral from which sand and glass are made, out of the soil and deposit it in their leaves. Silica makes the leaves gritty, and a grazer that chews them day after day finds its teeth gradually worn down. Experiments on voles have shown that animals fed on grasses with a higher silica content grew more slowly, and some researchers believe that the evolution of hard-wearing teeth in grazing animals is, in part, a response to this armour built from the soil itself. The contest, in other words, has been going on for so long that it has shaped both sides.

C  Chemical weapons are even more varied. Plants manufacture many thousands of compounds, among them the nicotine of tobacco, the caffeine of coffee and the tannins that make unripe fruit taste bitter and dry the mouth. Many of these substances are poisons or deterrents to insects, and the plants that make them are usually avoided. A neat trick is practised by mustard and its relatives, which include cabbage and horseradish. Their leaves contain harmless-looking compounds stored in one set of cells, and an enzyme stored in another. Only when a caterpillar bites through the tissue do the two meet, and the result is a burst of pungent mustard oil, the same sharpness that we taste in wasabi. The plant, in effect, keeps a bomb that is armed only when it is attacked, which means that it need not risk poisoning itself.

D  More surprising still is the discovery that plants can call for help. When caterpillars chew on maize leaves, the plant releases a blend of airborne chemicals that attracts parasitic wasps, which lay their eggs in the caterpillars and so destroy them. Nor is the message necessarily private. In experiments on sagebrush, a desert shrub, neighbouring plants that were exposed to the scent of damaged leaves suffered less damage from grazing insects over the following season than those that were not, suggesting that they had picked up the warning and prepared themselves. More recently, researchers have found that some plants can even detect the vibrations made by a chewing caterpillar. They respond to the sound of munching by increasing their production of mustard oil, whereas recordings of wind or of insect song provoke no such reaction, so the plants appear able to tell a threat from harmless noise.

E  Some plants go further and hire bodyguards. Several species of acacia in Africa and Central America grow swollen, hollow thorns in which ants can nest, and they provide nectar from glands on their leaves as a supply of food. In return, the ants swarm out to attack anything that touches the tree, from leaf-eating beetles to much larger animals. A long-term experiment in Kenya found that when ants were kept off acacia trees, elephants browsed them far more heavily than they did trees with ants in residence, and the unprotected trees grew more slowly. Tiny insects, it seems, can be better defenders than any thorn. The arrangement is not without its own costs, since the tree must feed its guardians all year round, and it breaks down in places where the ants are driven out by invading species.

F  Defence, however, has a price. Producing toxins and thorns uses energy and raw materials that might otherwise go into growth and seeds, so many plants rely on what are called induced defences, which they make only after an attack has begun. This has implications for farming. When people domesticated crops, they favoured plants that tasted sweeter and less bitter, and in doing so often bred out some of the defensive compounds. Modern crops are therefore more vulnerable to pests than their wild relatives, and farmers compensate with pesticides. Plant scientists are now looking at wild relatives for traits, such as the ability to call wasps, that might be reintroduced, offering a way to protect harvests with less chemical spraying. The compounds that deter insects have also given us medicines: salicylic acid from willow bark is the ancestor of aspirin, and plants remain one of the richest sources of new drugs.

passages.title: Who owns the Moon? The case for and against space mining
paras: A  In 2015 the United States passed a law giving American companies the right to own whatever they extract from asteroids. Luxembourg followed in 2017, and the United Arab Emirates and Japan have since passed their own versions. For years such legislation looked like the fantasy of space enthusiasts. Today it is described as the starting gun of the next gold rush, and a few dozen companies around the world have declared their intention to prospect among the planets and moons of the solar system. Whether they will succeed is far from clear. What is certain is that the legal and ethical questions will not wait for the technology.

B  The headline claims are dramatic. A single asteroid, we are told, may contain metals worth trillions of dollars. I find such figures meaningless. They are obtained by multiplying the mass of an asteroid by the price of platinum on Earth today, which ignores the obvious fact that if even a fraction of that metal were delivered to the market, its price would collapse. The sums also ignore the difficulty of the journey. It is the expense of fighting Earth's gravity that dominates every space project, and the cost of lifting a single kilogram of cargo into orbit, although it has fallen, is still counted in thousands of pounds. Any scheme that depends on flying large amounts of metal back to Earth, to be sold at a profit, should be viewed with suspicion.

C  The sounder case, in my view, concerns resources that would be used in space itself. Water is the obvious candidate. It is found as ice in permanently shadowed craters near the Moon's poles and in some kinds of asteroid, and it can be split into hydrogen and oxygen, the ingredients of rocket fuel. Fuel made in space would not have to be hauled up out of Earth's gravity at enormous expense; a spacecraft bound for Mars could refuel on the way, much as a lorry stops at a motorway service station. Water for astronauts to drink and air for them to breathe could be obtained in the same way. I would expect water, not gold or platinum, to be the first resource mined at a profit beyond Earth, and the customers will be other space companies, not people on the ground.

D  The legal position is murkier than the enthusiasts admit. The Outer Space Treaty of 1967, which most of the world's nations have signed, forbids any country from claiming sovereignty over the Moon or other celestial bodies, but it says nothing explicit about whether a company may keep what it digs up. Supporters of the new laws argue that taking resources is not the same as owning territory, much as a fishing boat owns the fish it catches but not the ocean. Critics reply that this is a convenient reading of an ambiguous text. It seems to me that both sides can make a respectable case, and that is precisely the problem: an agreement that two opposing readings can fit is a poor foundation on which to invest billions.

E  National laws cannot settle the matter. A statute passed in Washington or Luxembourg binds its own companies and nobody else, and it would be absurd for rival nations to develop rival rules for the same crater. Some countries have tried a different route in the Artemis Accords, drawn up in 2020 under American leadership. These set out principles for lunar exploration, among them that extracting resources is permitted and that safety zones may be established around operations. The accords are a useful start, but they are not a treaty. They bind nobody in law, and several major spacefaring nations have declined to sign them. A club of like-minded states is no substitute for rules that apply to everyone.

F  Opponents of space mining raise other objections, and some of them deserve a hearing. Astronomers worry that dust and activity might ruin the far side of the Moon, which is shielded from the radio noise of Earth and is therefore one of the best places in the solar system from which to listen to the early universe. Others argue that sites such as the Apollo landing areas are part of humanity's heritage and should be left undisturbed. I am sympathetic to both points; setting aside a small number of protected sites would cost little and would reassure many. Less persuasive is the argument, sometimes made by the industry itself, that mining asteroids will spare the environment of Earth. Most of the minerals extracted on our planet are cheap and plentiful, and it is hard to imagine anyone hauling them from space to save a hillside in Chile.

G  So where does that leave us? Not with a ban, which would be impossible to enforce and would deny humanity the benefits of cheaper space travel. Nor with the present free-for-all, in which ambition runs ahead of the rules. What is needed is a binding international agreement, negotiated before anyone has a mine to defend. It is far easier to agree on rules when nobody has anything to lose than after claims have been staked and fortunes invested. Half a century ago the nations of the world managed to write a treaty for space when almost nobody could reach it. They should be able to manage another now, while the prospectors are still only drawing up their plans.
